Research Project · 2024

Science Museum London

Redesigning the “Who Am I?” exhibit experience. A university research project: observing how visitors use the gallery, synthesising the insights, and proposing design improvements that hold attention and personalise the visit.

DisciplineUser Research · UX · Ethnography
TeamIndependent project
OutcomeDesign proposals · Process book
TimelineNov 2024 – Jan 2025

The brief

The brief asked me to frame my design process as a case study: run secondary research and in-context observation at the Science Museum London, define a problem space, generate insights, and propose informed design solutions, documenting the journey throughout.

01Research

Understanding the museum and its visitors

Before designing anything, I set out to understand the museum, the “Who Am I?” gallery, and how real people move through it, pairing literature review with in-context observation.

Secondary research

Before visiting, I ran a literature review. I explored the Science Museum’s history, values, competitors and visitor data, and looked closely at the “Who Am I?” exhibit itself.

Ethics: considerations & implications

I ran ethnographically-inspired research using non-participant covert observation, watching natural behaviour in a real-world context. That method carries real trade-offs, which I weighed up front.

Considerations

  • Keep data anonymous so no participant can be identified.
  • Minimise intrusion by observing only public, low-privacy areas.
  • Disclose the methodology and its justification openly.

Implications

  • Observing people in sensitive moments can intrude on their privacy.
  • Mishandled data could cause emotional or social harm.
  • Covert observation removes participants' autonomy to opt out.
  • Public trust in research can suffer if covert methods feel unfair.

Primary & secondary research

My research spanned three literature reviews (the museum, UX in public spaces, and my research question), exhibit layout diagrams, and in-context user observations.

Trajectory & sensory maps

To go deeper, I mapped the space itself. I followed three groups of visitors to build a trajectory map of their routes, and layered a sensory map of visual, touch and sound interactions across the gallery.

Consolidated findings

Everything converged on a tight set of findings, and from them, two clear pain points and one guiding question.

Consolidated findings
01

High-Traffic Areas : The most frequently visited sections were My Feelings, What Are You Afraid Of?, Seating areas, and My Body.

02

Interactions : The game at “My Brain” intrigued most kids because of its use of a camera, and where adults were clicking pictures with family and friends.

03

Proximity & Convenience : Visitors gravitated toward the nearest exhibits from the entrance, suggesting that convenience played a key role in navigation.

04

Dominance of Visual Stimuli : Visitors, especially children, were most drawn to visual elements, while scents and smells were not used in the experience of the exhibit.

Short Engagement Span

Visitors showed low attention spans and short interaction times at each screen.

Parental Supervision

Parents had to guide their children through the game, hinting at a usability gap.

Guiding question

How can technology help enhance visitor engagement and attention in museums?

The problem, in simple words

02Proposal

From insight to intervention

With the problem framed, I moved into ideation, benchmarking what already exists and shaping two proposals that answer the pain points directly.

01
Proposal idea

Personalised Customer Journey

A QR-code sign-up with a facial-recognition system that personalises the visit. It uses simple data like age to tailor games and activities to different skill levels, tracks progress, greets each visitor, and hands back a summary of key takeaways at the end.

Documents your visit
Key takeaways
Post-visit engagement
Modifies difficulty
Enhances engagement
Primary users

Museum visitors

Stakeholders
VisitorsMuseum adminThe organisationMarketingIT / developmentPartners & vendors

How it answers the pain points

Modifying difficulty levels — age-appropriate, comprehensible games that remove the need for parental supervision

Personalisation — tailoring the experience to individual needs so visitors feel valued and engaged

Post-visit engagement — key takeaways that drive higher retention after the visit

SWOT analysis

S

Strengths

  • Personalisation of the whole experience
  • Intuitive access; facial recognition for quick, personal greetings
  • Progress tracking that adds value to the visit
  • A more educational, memorable experience
W

Weaknesses

  • High initial cost of the recognition tech and upkeep
  • Privacy concerns around facial-data storage
  • Heavy dependence on technology
  • Limited access for visitors without smartphones
O

Opportunities

  • Rich analytics on visitor preferences
  • Scalable and adaptable to other galleries
T

Threats

  • Competing attractions and experiences
  • Fast-moving competition in interactive tech

Competitive analysis

I felt the exhibit lacked key takeaways to reinforce learning for children, and saw personalisation as the lever to raise engagement. Before committing, I benchmarked existing products that use personalisation, comparing how they approach it and what I could borrow, particularly around tailoring the experience and sending people away with something to keep.

National Gallery Singapore Generative AI guide

High personalisation
Key features
  • Hyper-personalised generative AI
  • Dynamic content delivery
  • Inclusive
Strengths
  • Real-time, hyper-personalised interactions
  • Scalable and adaptable technology
  • Adaptability based on user preferences, making it inclusive
  • Deep, interactive storytelling
Weaknesses
  • Reliant on advanced technology
  • Does not cater to less tech-savvy people, like the elderly
  • Constant updating and AI training required to stay relevant
Cost

Initial investment and maintenance costs will be high.

Natural History Museum London NaturePlus

Low personalisation
Key features
  • After-visit digital engagement
  • Collection of artifacts
  • News & events engagement online
Strengths
  • Shared knowledge and collaborative learning
  • Fostering discussions
  • Improved digital presence
Weaknesses
  • Inactive currently
  • Outdated platform and lack of any dynamic personalisation
Cost

Low cost.

Museum of Discovery (University of South Australia) Token

Medium personalisation
Key features
  • Token system
  • Interactive questions
  • Reflective, personalised summary
Strengths
  • Simplified technology, accessible for all visitor demographics
  • Promotes active participation and self-reflection
  • After-visit engagement with educational takeaways to view
Weaknesses
  • Technology is less advanced
  • Personalisation and customisation limited to predefined conditions or games
Cost

Low cost.
